sections.title: Why hold data back?
paragraphs: Training updates a {{model}}'s {{weights}} using examples it studies. If you measure success on those same examples, you are grading an open-book exam.

The {{model}} might score perfectly on training rows by {{memorization}} — repeating answers it has seen — without learning a rule that works on new data. That gap is why we care about {{generalization}}.
So we split data. Most rows go in the {{trainSet}}; the {{model}} is allowed to learn from these. A separate {{testSet}} stays locked away until evaluation time.
Performance on the {{testSet}} estimates how the {{model}} will behave on new, unseen {{input}}s. It is the honest report card.
Getting this split right matters before you trust any accuracy number — including when you later evaluate language models in AiEval.
bullets: High test performance — evidence of real {{generalization}}, not just {{memorization}}.

check.prompt: You train on all 1,000 customer reviews and report accuracy on those same 1,000 reviews. What is the main problem?
check.answer: You cannot tell if the model generalizes to new customers
choices: You cannot tell if the model generalizes to new customers
Test sets are only for image models
1,000 examples is always too few to train
check.explanation: Training and testing on the same rows measures {{memorization}}, not {{generalization}}. New customers bring new wording — you need a {{testSet}} the {{model}} never trained on.

sections.title: The memorization trap
paragraphs: Imagine studying for a quiz by copying only the ten practice questions. You might score 100% on those ten — and fail on question eleven.
{{model}}s do the same. A tiny network can memorize every XOR row and still fail on a slightly different layout.
That is why we never trust training accuracy alone. We want performance on held-out data the {{model}} did not use to update {{weights}}.
There is a second trap: peeking at the {{testSet}} while tuning {{hyperparameters}}. If you keep adjusting until the test score looks best, the test set stops being honest.
In practice teams use a {{validationSet}} for tuning and keep the {{testSet}} for a final report. The principle stays the same: measure on what was not used for training decisions.

reveals.prompt: Scenario: Train on all 1,000 reviews, report on same 1,000 → Result?
reveals.reveal: Misleadingly high — you cannot tell if the {{model}} achieves real {{generalization}} on new customers.

reveals.prompt: Scenario: Train on 800, evaluate on 200 never seen during training → Result?
reveals.reveal: A fairer signal — the 200 test reviews simulate new data.

reveals.prompt: Scenario: Peek at the {{testSet}}, tune {{hyperparameters}} until test score is best → Result?
reveals.reveal: You leaked the {{testSet}} into your decisions — use a {{validationSet}} for tuning instead.

check.prompt: You keep tweaking prompts until your eval hits 98% on the same 20 questions you practice on daily. What is the main risk?
check.answer: You may have overfit those 20 — performance on new questions could be much worse.
choices: The model is definitely ready for production.
You may have overfit those 20 — performance on new questions could be much worse.
Test sets are only needed for image models.
20 questions is always too small to learn anything.
check.explanation: You tuned to a tiny {{trainSet}} of prompts. The score reflects {{memorization}} of those 20, not {{generalization}} to new tasks. Hold out fresh questions for an honest {{testSet}}.

sections.title: How to split in practice
paragraphs: There is no magic ratio for every project, but the workflow is consistent: shuffle, hold out a chunk for testing, train only on the rest, and touch the {{testSet}} rarely for final reporting.
A common starting point for small tabular datasets is roughly 80% {{trainSet}} and 20% {{testSet}}. Larger datasets may use smaller test fractions.
Never tune {{hyperparameters}} by watching {{testSet}} accuracy climb — that contaminates the test set and makes the score optimistic.

Try the optional **Train vs test lab** from this lesson if you want a hands-on split. The **Neural network lab** trains on every row later — a shortcut so you can focus on {{loss}} and {{weights}} first.
In real projects and in AiEval evaluations, always ask: was this score computed on data the {{model}} never trained on?
bullets: Shuffle before splitting so the {{testSet}} is representative.
Tune on a {{validationSet}}, not the final {{testSet}}.
Report {{testSet}} performance once you are ready to decide.

check.prompt: You have 1,000 labeled emails. What is the cleanest way to report how well a spam filter generalizes?
check.answer: Train on a random subset, evaluate on held-out emails never used in training
choices: Train and evaluate on all 1,000 emails
Train on a random subset, evaluate on held-out emails never used in training
Shuffle labels randomly so the model sees more variety
Delete half the data so training is faster
check.explanation: The {{testSet}} must be unseen during training. Training and evaluating on the same 1,000 rows only shows {{memorization}}. A held-out split simulates new mail.

recapQuestions.prompt: In one phrase: what is the {{testSet}} for?
accept: honest evaluation on held out data
to see how well it generalizes
recapQuestions.explanation: The {{testSet}} is your honest estimate of {{generalization}}. It must stay separate from the {{trainSet}} so you measure pattern learning, not {{memorization}}.

recapQuestions.prompt: Your team tunes prompt wording every day until 30 benchmark questions score perfectly. What should you do next before claiming production readiness?
recapQuestions.answer: Evaluate on a fresh held-out question set never used during tuning
choices: Ship immediately — 100% on benchmarks is enough
Evaluate on a fresh held-out question set never used during tuning
Merge the benchmark into training data
Stop using a test set to save time
recapQuestions.explanation: The 30 questions became a contaminated {{trainSet}} through repeated tuning. A fresh {{testSet}} checks whether the prompt {{generalization}}izes beyond those familiar rows.
